questions.prompt: Why does Yjs use stable IDs `(clientId, clock)` instead of timestamps to resolve concurrent inserts?

options.label: Timestamps need wall-clock synchronization across machines, which is unreliable; stable IDs are local-monotonic and total-ordered without coordination
Stable IDs are smaller than 64-bit timestamps in memory
Timestamps can't represent insertions that happen in the same millisecond
Yjs predates the JavaScript Date API supporting nanoseconds

questions.explanation: Clock skew between clients makes timestamp ordering unreliable, and timestamp ties still need a tiebreaker. `(clientId, clock)` pairs are unique by construction (no two clients share a clientId), local-monotonic (clock only goes up), and impose a total order that every replica agrees on without coordination. The other options describe real but secondary benefits.

questions.prompt: What's the primary difference between state-based (CvRDT) and op-based (CmRDT) CRDTs?

options.label: State-based supports offline edits; op-based does not
State-based gossips the entire replica state and merges via lattice join; op-based broadcasts individual operations and requires causal delivery
State-based is for text; op-based is for counters
State-based runs on a single machine; op-based requires multiple machines

questions.explanation: The wire shape and ordering requirements are the split. State-based sends full state, joins are commutative/associative/idempotent by lattice structure, and order doesn't matter. Op-based sends individual ops and needs the transport to deliver them in causal order. Both deliver strong eventual consistency; they just trade bandwidth against ordering.

questions.prompt: When is it safe to construct a Y.Doc with `gc: true`?

options.label: Always — the GC is fully transparent and never has correctness implications
Only when there's only one peer (no real collaboration), so deletes never race with concurrent ops
When every peer has observed the deletions before any might come back online with stale ops — typically when sync windows are short (minutes to a few hours)
Only on the server, never on clients

questions.explanation: GC collapses tombstones once they're causally observed by all live replicas. If a long-offline peer reconnects later with ops that reference items the server has already GC'd, integration can fail. Short sync windows make this safe; long offline windows or full-history features (undo across days, audit replay) need `gc: false`.

questions.prompt: Roughly how does the memory cost of `Y.Text` with 100K characters compare to the same string as a plain JavaScript string?

options.label: Approximately the same
~3× the plain-string cost — each character lives in an Item block with origin pointers and metadata
~100× the plain-string cost — Yjs is fundamentally inefficient for text
Half the cost — Yjs uses binary encoding that beats UTF-16 strings

questions.explanation: The ~3× figure is the canonical number for editor-scale text. Items carry IDs, origin/rightOrigin pointers, content, and flags; the overhead per character is real but bounded. Heavily edited docs (tombstones + GC patterns) can go higher. Plain strings are cheaper, but they don't merge — that's the trade.

questions.prompt: What does 'strong eventual consistency' guarantee about CRDT replicas?

options.label: All replicas always have identical state at every instant
Replicas converge to the latest update, where 'latest' is determined by wall-clock timestamps
Any two replicas that have received the same set of updates are in the same state — independent of the order they arrived, because the merge function is commutative, associative, and idempotent
A central coordinator broadcasts a canonical order; replicas catch up to that order eventually

questions.explanation: SEC is order-independent convergence given the same op set. The three algebraic properties — commutative, associative, idempotent — are what let any application order, including duplicates, reach the same final state. Option (a) is too strong (instantaneous consistency); (b) and (d) describe last-write-wins and coordinated systems respectively, not CRDTs.
